Triggers.value: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel like I don't know myself anymore
Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
I can't rely on other people

issues.item: Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
issues.explanation: 'Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident' is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of natural disaster. A car-crash-specific trigger suggests a different index trauma unless there is clear disaster-related context, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Memory: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
issues.explanation: 'Rage on Recall' is not well supported by the rest of the profile, which otherwise centers on fear, vulnerability, dissociation/gaps, and interpersonal mistrust after a natural disaster. Intense rage could occur clinically, but here it lacks corroboration from threat or appraisal items and weakens overall coherence.

For a natural disaster trauma, 'related people' as a primary trigger is hard to justify unless they were directly linked to the event; with no supporting interpersonal trauma content elsewhere, this trigger is clinically questionable.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
issues.explanation: The threat item about unusual silence implying imminent danger fits combat/interpersonal danger contexts more than natural disaster exposure, and it is not supported by the trigger or appraisal content here.

vignette:
Liam Kowalski is a 29-year-old Polish-American salesperson who presented for psychological assessment approximately eight months after surviving a catastrophic flash flood that struck a rural campsite in the Pacific Northwest where he had been vacationing alone. He had been sleeping in a tent near a riverbank when the water rose with almost no warning in the early hours of the morning. He described clawing his way out of the tent as it collapsed around him, being swept downstream in near-total darkness, colliding with debris, and clinging to a fallen tree for what he estimated was close to two hours before rescuers reached him. Throughout that time he had no certainty he would survive, and the roaring of the water, the cold, and the absolute isolation of those hours appear to have constituted the core of his traumatic experience.

In the weeks following the flood, Liam noticed that certain sensory encounters could pull him back into the terror of that night with startling immediacy. Driving past a river on a sales route through the Central Valley, catching a particular smell of damp earth on a client's property, or simply finding himself in any wooded or natural setting would produce a visceral re-experiencing - suddenly he was not in his car or on a doorstep but back in the dark current, certain he was going to die. These flashbacks arrived without warning and carried the same terror he had felt clinging to that tree, not as a recollection but as a present event. On nights following such encounters he would wake repeatedly, sitting upright in the dark to listen for sounds he could not quite name, his body convinced that danger was still close. He had come to move through the world in a state of near-constant watchfulness, scanning his environment in ways he recognised as excessive but could not suppress.

What complicated Liam's recovery most profoundly was the fragmentary and emotionally volatile nature of his memories of the flood itself. There are portions of those two hours he simply cannot retrieve - gaps that feel less like forgetting and more like an absence he cannot see around. At other times, with no clear image attached, the full emotional weight of the event would descend on him without context: a wave of cold dread and helplessness that seemed to come from nowhere. When he did try to recall the event deliberately, the terror returned at its original intensity, and this made memory itself feel dangerous. These intrusive emotional states fed directly into his sense that something had permanently broken in him, reinforcing his belief that he was no longer the person he had been before the flood. The fragmented, uncontrolled quality of his remembering also meant that any cue resembling the flood - a trail map on a colleague's desk, a nature documentary playing in a waiting room - could trigger a renewed flood of distressing emotion, as though the incomplete memory were perpetually searching for a way back in.

Over the months since the event, Liam's appraisals of himself and his world had darkened considerably. He had come to believe that he could not rely on other people - that the isolation of those two hours had revealed something true about his fundamental aloneness - and this conviction had led him to withdraw from the modest social network he had maintained. He was certain that nothing in his life held meaning anymore, and this pervasive emptiness made it harder to resist the pull of threat monitoring: if nothing mattered and no one could be counted on, then vigilance was the only rational response. His negative appraisals also amplified the potency of his triggers; because he now saw himself as permanently damaged and the world as fundamentally unsafe, even mild emotional vulnerability - a moment of loneliness during a long sales drive - could itself become a trigger, flooding him with the helplessness he had felt in the water. This loop had tightened steadily. His hypervigilance and fragmented memories confirmed his worst beliefs about himself, and those beliefs in turn kept him scanning, kept him waking at night, kept him reading ordinary situations as harbingers of catastrophe.

Liam sought help after declining a regional sales promotion that would have required travel through mountainous terrain. He told the intake clinician that he had once considered himself adventurous and self-sufficient, and that turning down that opportunity was the moment he could no longer pretend he was managing. What he most feared, he said quietly, was that the person he used to be was simply gone. What he most hoped was that someone could tell him otherwise.
